title: Algorithmic Management and its Impact on Employee Autonomy, Job Satisfaction, and Performance

detail.title: Algorithmic Management and its Impact on Employee Autonomy, Job Satisfaction, and Performance
detail.abstract:
The growing use of algorithm based systems to manage employees has transformed how work is organized and controlled in contemporary organizations. Commonly referred to as algorithmic management, this approach relies on automated decision making to allocate tasks, monitor performance, and evaluate employee outcomes. While such systems are often adopted to enhance efficiency, their implications for human work remain insufficiently understood. This study examined the relationship between algorithmic management and key employee outcomes, with a particular focus on employee autonomy, job satisfaction, and performance. 
Using a quantitative research design, data were collected through an online survey from employees working in algorithmically managed environments. Established measurement scales were employed to assess the study variables, and statistical analyses were conducted to test the proposed hypotheses. The findings indicate that algorithmic management is negatively associated with employee autonomy and job satisfaction, while demonstrating a significant relationship with employee performance. These results suggest that algorithmic management may improve performance related outcomes but can also constrain employees' sense of control and satisfaction at work. 
The study contributes to the growing literature on digital and technology-mediated management by highlighting the dual effects of algorithmic management on human work. From a practical perspective, the findings underscore the importance of designing algorithmic systems that balance organizational efficiency with employee well-being. The study also offers directions for future research on the evolving role of algorithms in shaping the future of work.

title: How Far Does Competition Travel? Causal Evidence on Localized Competition in In-Store and Curbside Pickup Operations
affiliations: and Miami University of Ohio - Department of Economics

detail.title: How Far Does Competition Travel? Causal Evidence on Localized Competition in In-Store and Curbside Pickup Operations
detail.abstract: Problem definition: In today's grocery environment, store managers are responsible for both traditional in-store operations and curbside pickup, a newer service innovation managed jointly at the store level. Yet little is known about how far competition travels in these linked channels or whether competition in one channel affects the other. Understanding these localized, cross-channel dynamics is essential for store managers to allocate resources effectively and make informed operational decisions. Methodology / results: We develop a stylized spatial-decay model to quantify how competitive effects attenuate with distance across the two co-located service channels. The model captures same-location and distance-based competition, providing a continuous measure of geographic reach for in-store and curbside pickup. Identification leverages competitor entry events, including new store openings and curbside pickup introductions, while an innovative instrumental variables approach is employed to address entry endogeneity. The analysis yields three key findings: (1) Curbside pickup does not extend the competitive radius as commonly assumed. Its estimated radius is about 1.7 miles, comparable to the 1.5-mile radius for in-store competition. (2) Cross-channel effects, often presumed substantial, appear only for stores without curbside pickup, consistent with a temporary first-mover advantage rather than pervasive cross-channel competition. (3) Ignoring endogeneity understates nearby effects and overstates distant effects, underscoring the importance of causal identification in spatial-competition research. Managerial implications: The findings provide actionable guidance for store managers and strategists. Because competition is highly localized, resource adjustments such as staffing, capacity, and promotions should focus on stores facing nearby rivals rather than distributed broadly. Minimal cross-channel substitution implies that in-store and curbside pickup operations can be managed independently, improving planning efficiency and performance evaluation. Strategically, retailers should update siteselection and network-planning models to reflect the narrow geographic reach of service-based channels and rely on data-driven spatial analysis rather than intuition when evaluating new openings, curbside retrofits, or fulfillment co-locations.

title: Experimentation, Biased Learning, and Conjectural Variations in Competitive Dynamic Pricing
affiliations: Business School, National University of Singapore and

detail.title: Experimentation, Biased Learning, and Conjectural Variations in Competitive Dynamic Pricing
detail.abstract: We study competitive dynamic pricing among multiple sellers, motivated by the rise of large-scale experimentation and algorithmic pricing in retail and online marketplaces. Sellers repeatedly set prices using simple learning rules and observe only their own prices and realized demand, even though demand depends on all sellers' prices and is subject to random shocks. Each seller runs two-point A/B price experiments, in the spirit of switchback-style designs, and updates a baseline price using a linear demand estimate fitted to its own data. Under certain conditions on demand, the resulting dynamics converge to a Conjectural Variations (CV) equilibrium, a classic static equilibrium notion in which each seller best responds under a conjecture that rivals' prices respond systematically to changes in its own price. Unlike standard CV models that treat conjectures as behavioral primitives, we show that these conjectures arise endogenously from the bias in demand learning induced by correlated experimentation (e.g., due to synchronized repricing schedules). This learning bias selects the long-run equilibrium, often leading to supra-competitive prices. Notably, we show that under independent experimentation, this bias vanishes and the learning dynamics converge to the standard Nash equilibrium. We provide simple sufficient conditions on demand for convergence in standard models and establish a finite-sample guarantee: up to logarithmic factors, the squared price error decays on the order of $T^{-1/2}$. Our results imply that in competitive markets, experimentation design can serve as a market design lever, selecting the equilibrium reached by practical learning algorithms.

title: A Relational Analogical Knowledge Assessment Theory Under Uncertainty with a Guardrail Based Framework

detail.title: A Relational Analogical Knowledge Assessment Theory Under Uncertainty with a Guardrail Based Framework
detail.abstract: Analogical reasoning-the science of similarity and comparison-is indispensable in domains where evidence is sparse, delayed, or incomplete. Classical Dempster-Shafer Theory (DST) provides a principled foundation for reasoning under uncertainty, but it becomes unstable when evidence is weak or or when systems exhibit time-delayed reaction. This work arises from the need to make reliable engineering decisions when evidence is sparse, uncertain, and must be interpreted through causation-aware analogical reasoning. The objective of this paper is to develop a theory of Relational Analogical Knowledge Assessment that integrates causal-relational structure, coarse-grained belief representation, and temporal evidence evolution, and to construct a guardrail framework that stabilizes belief fusion under sparse or uncertain evidence using expert-defined thresholds and dependability classes that map analogical proximity into operational fusion strategies. The method further constructs a framework by modeling a causal relational skeleton, defining an operator that evaluates analogical proximity and restricts evidence transfer to causally valid pathways, and representing uncertainty through coarse-grained belief states that stabilize reasoning under sparse or noisy data. It incorporates a belief-evolution mechanism to handle temporally unfolding evidence and delayed system reactions, and embeds a guardrail framework that detects and mitigates unstable or inappropriate belief updates. The approach further incorporates expert-defined thresholds and dependability classes to translate analogical distance into context-appropriate fusion strategies, yielding a causation-aware, guardrail-stabilized extension of DST for reliable analogical reasoning in engineering settings. The application of this approach are highly relevant to process-engineering domains involving geological, chemical, or biological systems, e.g., oil and gas operations, pipeline integrity management, grain preservation, drug discovery or complex medical treatments. This research aligns with the ongoing development of a theoretical foundation for the patented CausX AI framework that is being adopted in the oil and gas industry, laying the groundwork for a progressively more robust and unified paradigm applicable to other high stake engineering domains.

detail.abstract:
In today's era where digital transformation reshapes the global business landscape, information security has transcended the boundaries of IT departments, evolving into a strategic challenge critical to the survival of all enterprises. Yet a harsh reality confronts us: for the SMB sector—the backbone of global economic resilience—establishing an effective information security governance system often feels like scaling an insurmountable mountain without supplies. Looking at today's security market, neither macro frameworks like NIST/ISO—tailored for enterprise-level organizations—nor premium professional consulting services, nor the ever-evolving technology stacks have fundamentally resolved the governance impasse SMBs face: “unaffordable, unmanageable, and unprotectable.” The industry has long suffered from a supply-demand mismatch, leaving SMBs without a guidance system that is both truly actionable and commercially viable.


The core insight of this paper is this: The collapse of security governance in SMBs often stems not from a lack of technology itself, but from the industry's long-standing technology-centric mindset, which obscures the critical governance variable of “human factors“ in governance. The author contends that enterprises can build a more resilient and cost-effective defense line than by piling up expensive hardware, even under conditions of severely constrained budgets and scarce resources—provided that their defensive focus is precisely anchored on the “human factor”.


Based on this, this paper conducts an in-depth analysis of the systemic failures of current mainstream security solutions when applied to SMBs. It also introduces, for the first time, an innovative, risk-centric theoretical model: Human-Centered Security Governance (HCSG). HCSG is not a watered-down version of traditional frameworks but a new paradigm built on three strategic pillars: asymmetric advantage, the 80/20 rule, and iterative evolution. Through three pragmatic steps—Minimized Identification, Minimized Deployment, and Minimized Iteration—it charts a sustainable evolutionary path for SMBs. Its underlying logic is remarkably simple yet powerful: rather than forcing a “farmer” to bankrupt himself buying tanks he cannot
master (a metaphor for imposing enterprise-scale solutions on SMBs), equipping him with a sophisticated “individual combat system” represents the optimal strategic choice to enhance his survival odds on the digital battlefield.


Finally, this paper earnestly calls upon all industry stakeholders to jointly advance the standardization of the HCSG toolkit. Using this as a connecting thread, we must build an inclusive security ecosystem with deep participation from insurance providers, IT service firms, and government agencies—systemically reshaping the defensive DNA of global SMBs.

title:
The American Premium Puzzle in Frictional Markets 
An Analytic Integral Representation of the Exit Right

detail.title:
The American Premium Puzzle in Frictional Markets 
An Analytic Integral Representation of the Exit Right
detail.abstract: Empirical studies document that American call options trade at a substantial premium— approximately 5.0–5.9%—over otherwise identical European contracts, a magnitude that standard dividend-based models, which predict premia on the order of 0.05%, fail to explain. We address this long-standing pricing puzzle by reinterpreting the early-exercise feature not as a dividend-capture device, but as a liquidity-driven Exit Right that allows option holders to bypass illiquid secondary markets when bid–ask spreads widen. Rather than modeling early exercise as an optimal stopping problem, we value this Exit Right as the ex ante, discounted expectation of avoided liquidation losses over the life of the contract. Under standard risk-neutral dynamics, the resulting liquidity premium admits a semi-analytic representation in the form of a time-weighted univariate Gaussian integral. Unlike boundary-based or replication-driven approaches that rely on compound options or free-boundary partial differential equations, our framework remains computationally lightweight while preserving analytic differentiability for hedging. Importantly, the model generates liquidity premia of the same order of magnitude as those observed in the data, providing a parsimonious and economically grounded resolution of the “unexplained residual” in American option prices.

Financial Planning & Analysis (FP&A) teams continue to rely heavily on Microsoft Excel for planning, forecasting, and management reporting, despite the volume of financial data exceeding traditional spreadsheet limits. As transactional systems scale and planning cycles accelerate, many FP&A workflows fail not during advanced modeling, but earlier in the process at data ingestion, preparation, and refresh. These breakdowns are typically caused by unstable file-based inputs, limited data validation, weak auditability, and insufficient visibility into data refresh reliability.
This paper presents a practical, cloud-native FP&A data pipeline designed to extend spreadsheet-first analysis while introducing engineering-grade reliability and scalability. The proposed architecture integrates Python-based bulk data ingestion, PostgreSQL as a scalable relational database, and Excel Power Query as the primary interface for analysis and consumption. This design enables FP&A teams to work with multi-million-row financial datasets while preserving familiar Excel workflows and avoiding premature migration to complex data warehouses or business intelligence platforms.
Empirical performance benchmarks using 2 million and 4 million row datasets demonstrate consistent ingestion times, predictable refresh behavior, and repeatable execution, making them suitable for operational FP&A use cases. The paper also proposes a forward-looking design to support datasets exceeding 10 million rows, emphasizing horizontal scalability, data reduction, and aggregation strategies aligned with real-world FP&A decision-making patterns. Overall, this research shows how modern data engineering principles can be applied within Excel-centric environments to improve reliability, transparency, and scale in FP&A operations

title: Working Paper No. 5: “Organisational Succession as a Risk Event: Continuity Failure, Value Erosion and the Limits of Planning”

detail.title: Working Paper No. 5: “Organisational Succession as a Risk Event: Continuity Failure, Value Erosion and the Limits of Planning”
detail.abstract: This working paper extends the Organisational Succession Science working paper series by reframing organisational succession as a critical organisational risk event. Existing governance and enterprise risk management frameworks typically treat succession as a procedural matter, subsumed within contingency planning or human capital; this framing over privileges structural sufficiency and under theorises legitimacy, authority and relational continuity. Building on the Structural, Psychological and Relational (SPR) lens and the OSI Legitimacy Model developed in earlier working papers, the paper conceptualises succession risk as multidimensional and systemic. It argues that continuity failure and value erosion often follow successions that are formally planned yet weakly legitimised, because authority must be designated, psychologically inhabited and relationally enacted across time. The paper develops an analytical account of structural risk, psychological risk and relational risk, and shows how misalignment across these domains amplifies exposure through slow decay, drift and fragmentation rather than immediate collapse. It then considers the implications for governance and stewardship, arguing that succession requires a different interpretive frame of responsibility without proposing prescriptive interventions. The paper closes by positioning succession risk as conceptual groundwork for later empirical investigation, including longitudinal study of succession outcomes within the wider research programme.

title: Margin and Cost Optimization Governance for Cloud and AI Businesses

detail.title: Margin and Cost Optimization Governance for Cloud and AI Businesses
detail.abstract:
As cloud, AI, and agentic systems reshape business economics, margin outcomes are increasingly influenced by usage behavior, cost-to-serve dynamics, and pricing decisions that evolve at different speeds. In these environments, traditional financial planning and reporting approaches often surface margin risk only after it has materialized, limiting the ability of finance leaders to intervene effectively.

This white paper presents a finance-led governance perspective for managing margin and cost dynamics in usage-driven business models. It outlines a governance model that connects operational usage signals, cost translation, scenario-based assessment, pricing alignment, and executive oversight to support earlier visibility and more deliberate decision making. The perspective synthesizes applied FP&A practices documented in industry case material into a generalized framework suitable for finance, analytics, and management leaders operating in technology-driven organizations.

The paper is intended as an executive reference rather than a technical or methodological contribution, emphasizing governance structure and decision readiness over forecasting precision or analytical techniques.

title: From the 15-Minute City to the Proximity Tourism Model: Adapting Urban Planning Concepts for Rural Mountain Destinations

detail.title: From the 15-Minute City to the Proximity Tourism Model: Adapting Urban Planning Concepts for Rural Mountain Destinations
detail.abstract: The 15-Minute City has emerged as a prominent urban planning model promoting sustainability, accessibility, and community well-being through proximity-based development. While extensively studied in metropolitan contexts, its applicability to rural and mountainous tourism destinations remains underexplored. This paper addresses this gap by conceptualizing an Experience Proximity Model that adapts core principles of the 15-Minute City to experience-based rural tourism settings. Using Hunza Valley in northern Pakistan as a qualitative case study, the research analyzes how organic settlement patterns, community-based tourism, and spatial clustering of services naturally reflect proximity principles without formal planning intervention. A comparative benchmarking analysis with selected global mountain destinations-Kiso Valley (Japan), Ghandruk (Nepal), Karakol CBT Region (Kyrgyzstan), and Busan (South Korea)-is employed to extract transferable lessons. Findings identify three core proximity dimensions relevant to rural tourism: (1) experiential accessibility through walkable clusters, (2) relational proximity via community-led tourism, and (3) polycentric spatial organization that distributes visitors while protecting sensitive environments. The study contributes theoretically by extending proximity planning beyond urban service delivery and practically by offering policy-relevant insights aligned with SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities) and SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production) for sustainable rural tourism development in mountain regions.

detail.abstract: This paper presents REBAPP, a web-based, multi-school education management platform designed and developed to support the Rohingya Education System (REBARAKAN). I led the system architecture and full-stack development of REBAPP using Next.js and the MERN stack. The platform is currently deployed in production and actively used by more than 60 Rohingya schools. REBAPP addresses critical challenges in refugee education including school governance, attendance integrity, curriculum distribution, performance monitoring, and parent-school communication. This case study demonstrates how locally built digital infrastructure can enable scalable, transparent, and accountable education systems for stateless and underserved communities.

title: Determinants of the Internationalization of Agrifood Firms: The Case of Olive Oil in Southern Spain
affiliations: University of Jaén and University of Jaén

detail.title: Determinants of the Internationalization of Agrifood Firms: The Case of Olive Oil in Southern Spain
detail.abstract: The aim of this article is to identify the conditions for the internationalization of olive oil producing firms in Southern Spain (province of Jaén), as this region accounts for 20 percent of total world production. To that end, we propose a model and test it with data from four premium extra virgin olive oil producing firms (two Born Globals and two non-Born Globals), combining a case study approach with Qualitative Comparative Analysis (QCA). The results show that firms must develop dynamic capabilities. To do so, firms must combine resources and capabilities; international market orientation, network orientation and entrepreneurship orientation strategies; and human, relational and technological capital. If this happens within the first three years of their incorporation, they can be Born Globals. These results can be extrapolated to other industries. Finally, this paper offers some policy implications for firms, such as: they should become more involved in facilitating the internationalization process for olive oil firms, promote the olive culture abroad, facilitate access to foreign markets, publicize the health benefits of extra virgin olive oil (EVOO).

title: Data-Driven Identification Method for Low-Voltage Distribution Station-User Relationships Based on Voltage Sequence Correlation
affiliations: Wuhan University of Technology and China Three Gorges University

detail.title: Data-Driven Identification Method for Low-Voltage Distribution Station-User Relationships Based on Voltage Sequence Correlation
detail.abstract: The actual connection relationships between distribution areas and users in low-voltage distribution networks form a critical foundation for metering management, line loss control, and electricity theft detection. However, the accuracy of these relationships has long faced significant challenges in many urban areas due to factors such as modifications to aging lines, delayed data updates, and changes in user wiring configurations.To address the high workload and low efficiency of traditional manual investigations, as well as the susceptibility to interference and limited penetration capabilities of specialized equipment like carrier-wave and pulse-current methods, this paper proposes a big data-driven identification method for transformer-user relationships. This approach utilizes voltage sequence data collected from both the low-voltage side and the user side via smart meters. By calculating the voltage similarity between users and the gateway meters of their transformer districts using Pearson correlation coefficients and significance probabilities, it identifies authentic transformer-user affiliations.Using Xingyuecheng Residential Community in Jiang'an District, Wuhan as a pilot site, data from 5 transformer districts and 1,150 households were analyzed. Voltage sequence data from 96 sampling points per day were examined.In the 253F1 transformer district, single-user test results from 672 sample points over 7 days showed a correlation coefficient of r=0.9948 and p=0 for users within the same district, while cross-district user correlation was only r=-0.0263 and p=0.4958. This demonstrates the method's effectiveness in distinguishing genuine from erroneous connections.During a large-scale test covering all 276 users in the 253F1 transformer district over 27 days (2,592 data points), 4 users with negative correlation values were identified, falling within the range (-0.16,-0.08).Subsequent verification confirmed that the voltage correlation between these 4 households and the 253F4 transformer district reached r≈0.9861-0.9921, confirming their actual district affiliation. The cumulative identification accuracy reached 100%. This method requires no additional hardware or power outages, significantly reducing field investigation costs and improving metering management efficiency in distribution networks. It holds high engineering application value and promising prospects for widespread adoption.

title: Research on First Article Inspection (FAI)-Driven Quality Assurance Methods for Wind Turbine Installation and Operation & Maintenance and Their Effect on Reliability Improvement

detail.title: Research on First Article Inspection (FAI)-Driven Quality Assurance Methods for Wind Turbine Installation and Operation & Maintenance and Their Effect on Reliability Improvement
detail.abstract: Variations in quality during the installation and early operational phases of wind turbines are a leading cause of unplanned shutdowns and reduced system reliability. To overcome the limitations of traditional quality control-which primarily relies on post-event checks and lacks a systematic, proactive mechanism-this paper proposes a First Article Inspection (FAI) approach tailored for both installation and maintenance stages. During the construction phase, an FAI inspection matrix is established for the first unit, focusing on critical parameters such as tower-flange bolt torque deviation, main shaft and gearbox alignment error, nacelle leveling, and consistency of key electrical connections. In the operation and maintenance phase, FAI is extended to a standardized validation checklist applied after each major maintenance task or technical upgrade, aimed at minimizing human operational deviations.An analysis of data from 23 wind farms and over 300 wind turbines demonstrates that implementing the FAI mechanism: (1) improves the first-pass installation rate by an average of 8.6% to 12.4%; (2) reduces unplanned outages within the first three months due to installation quality issues by over 25%; and (3) increases the post-repair unit availability by 1.5 to 2.3 percentage points on average. These results confirm that FAI, as a systematic and replicable proactive quality control framework, significantly enhances the operational reliability of wind turbines throughout their lifecycle.

title: The Importance of Endogenous Resources for Internationalization: Competitive Advantages in the Olive Groves of Southern Spain
affiliations: University of Jaén and University of Jaén

detail.title: The Importance of Endogenous Resources for Internationalization: Competitive Advantages in the Olive Groves of Southern Spain
detail.abstract: The general objective of this paper was to determine how companies in the olive sector could convert the comparative advantages of olive-growing regions (e.g., culture, tradition, raw materials, knowledge, infrastructure, networks, technological centers, etc.) into competitive advantages, to internationalize, in an accelerated way, and become born global firms, contributing to economic, social, and sustainable development of regions. Thus, we analyzed four cases of exporting companies in this sector (two born global and two non-born global) in southern Spain (Jaén). We chose this province because it is the world's leading producer of olive oil and, yet it is only the fourth largest exporter compared to the rest of Spain. For the case study, we conducted (and recorded) personal, semi-structured interviews with the founders/managers or individuals in charge of internationalization. To obtain our results, we used a data sheet that included an action protocol, we analyzed each case individually, and we employed sensemaking and pattern-matching techniques to add validity and reliability to the research. Finally, we proposed the "keys" for these companies to go international in an accelerated way, as it would increase their competitiveness, foster the creation of employment, develop networks between companies, boost investment in innovation, etc. The results indicate that it is necessary to follow market orientation, networking, and international entrepreneurship strategies, and that intellectual capital (human, organizational, relational, and technological) of companies (and, therefore, of regions) will be the means through which competitive capabilities are achieved.

detail.abstract: Aluminum packaging plays a critical role in modern food, beverage, pharmaceutical, and industrial supply chains due to its unique combination of barrier performance, mechanical reliability, thermal versatility, and recyclability. This paper provides a structured analytical overview of aluminum packaging based on industry and sectoral evidence, focusing on material characteristics, manufacturing formats, functional performance, and sustainability implications. Drawing on published industry fact sheets and packaging system descriptions, the study examines why aluminum remains a preferred packaging material despite competition from plastics, glass, and steel. The paper further evaluates aluminum packaging's contribution to shelf-life extension, transport efficiency, and circular economy frameworks, while also identifying limitations related to energy-intensive primary production and recycling dependency on infrastructure.

title: Wealth and Income Inequality Early in Life: Underage Children as Owners of Privately Held Firms
affiliations: VATT Institute for Economic Research and

detail.title: Wealth and Income Inequality Early in Life: Underage Children as Owners of Privately Held Firms
detail.abstract: Using unique administrative data that link privately held firm owners to rich background information, we provide novel evidence on underage children as firm owners. Ownership occurs at all ages 0--17, with a mean age of 12. Childhood ownership is strongly concentrated among high-income families, creates substantial early-life income flows and exacerbates intergenerational inequality. Firm-owning children have in their childhood average incomes which would place them in the fourth decile of the adult income distribution and which imply wealth holdings at the seventh wealth decile. At age 30, child owners are substantially overrepresented in their cohort’s top 1%.

title: Institutions and Climate Change
affiliations: University College London, , London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) and Institut d'Etudes Politiques de Paris (Sciences Po)

detail.title: Institutions and Climate Change
detail.abstract: This paper reviews research across economics, political economy, political science, and public policy to investigate how institutions shape the adoption, implementation, and durability of climate policies. We examine how formal institutions (i) coordinate implementation capacity, (ii) anchor long-term commitments, and (iii) mediate distributional conflict. We also discuss how informal institutions, such as social norms and trust, further condition whether formal mechanisms translate into durable action. We distinguish quasi-experimental evidence from correlational and case-based findings, identifying where economic methods could further sharpen evidence, and conclude with a research agenda focused on institutional interdependencies and the conditions under which institutions can facilitate the adoption of effective and irreversible climate policies.

title: Experts as Intermediaries
affiliations: Ifo Institute, University of Duisburg-Essen,  and

detail.title: Experts as Intermediaries
detail.abstract: Households often struggle to understand policy interventions, limiting the effectiveness of policy transmission. We study how economic policy signals reach and influence households, focusing on the role of professional economists as interpretive intermediaries. When policy signals are complex and households face attentional limits, experts help filter and explain the information. Using a series of large-scale cross-national expert surveys and representative household experiments in Germany during the 2022–23 inflation surge, we show that (i) experts actively update and interpret monetary policy signals, (ii) their policy interpretations influence household expectations and spending decisions, and (iii) households prefer expert interpretations over direct communication from policymakers. Our findings highlight a previously overlooked transmission channel, suggesting that expert intermediation can substantially enhance the effectiveness of macroeconomic policy communication.
